course_description:
This course is a critical examination of the legal and social issues that arise in the practice of human rights law. The course seeks to develop students' skills in critical analysis by encouraging them to reflect on the role of human rights law in protecting vulnerable people, shaping legislation and influencing public policy, and whether human rights law has the capability to solve complex social problems.

This course is a detailed examination of Australian human rights law.

You will be required to reflect on the influence that the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) has had on our local legal landscape.

You will have a chance to evaluate whether a federal Human Rights Act would have a positive effect on Australian law, and to analyse the effectiveness of current Commonwealth law in protecting human rights.

An important, but often overlooked, area of human rights law is anti-discrimination law, and you will receive a detailed overview of this important tool for protecting the rights of vulnerable people.

You will be required to apply the human rights law you learn to a range of Australian human rights issues, particularly those that are under-acknowledged and under-publicised, and you will learn what it means to take a 'rights-based approach' to legal practice.

The tutorials will be run as skills sessions. You will be encouraged to develop practical legal skills including client interviewing, legal drafting, advocacy and debate.

You will be assessed on your capacity to develop practical skills in oral communication, analysis, problem solving and legal writing. You will also be assessed on your professionalism through weekly reflective responses.ﾠ

course_aims:
Education Mission Statement

The mission of the School of Law is to educate you in and about the law. We seek to assist you to think critically about the law and to investigate its structures, principles, policies, and values. This is achieved by engaging with you as fellow investigators in a range of critical and intellectual conversations about the law and its place in society. Our role is thus to guide you in your own intellectual journey in the law and to equip you with the necessary skills that will enable you to continue that journey long after you have left the School.

Course Aims

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate knowledge of human rights laws (including anti-discrimination laws) and be able to apply them in domestic legal situations.
Determine the kinds of remedies that are available to defend human rights in a variety of domestic legal situations.
Appreciate the manner in which the law impacts upon vulnerable groups in Australia.
Work in a team to develop skills in human rights lawyering.
Apply a 'rights-based' approach to legal practice.

assessment_details.title: Phone a friend
assessment_details.task_description: Students will submit four (4) phone-a-friend templates. Students phone-a-friend (partners allocated in class) on four occasions throughout the semester to discuss the readings for that week. Prompt questions (if needed) are: What were your impressions? What did you learn from the readings? What didn’t you understand? Did you agree/disagree with what the author said/judge decided? The activity must be undertaken over the telephone. Not in person. Not via video conferencing. Phone calls must be 20-30 minutes long. Students can decide collaboratively which weeks they complete the exercise. For each phone conversation, students must complete a Phone-a-Friend Template (on the next page). One Template must be completed for each phone conversation, so four (4) templates must be submitted by the due date via Turnitin. Completing the template: Your notes should be akin to a file note (ie. a contemporaneous record of a discussion or event). I expect it to be well-expressed and clear, but less formal than an essay. You should describe what you talked about, what your view was, what your partner’s view was and what conclusions you came to. It can be in point form. No formal references/footnotes are required. For each entry, you must include: the date and time of the call; how long the call went for; your partner’s name. This is all provided for in the Template. Make sure you include any challenges you faced with this task – eg. not being able to reach your partner to make a time; not being able to reach your partner at the agreed time. If you are not a collegial partner, this will affect your mark, so please make sure you work together on this, and be committed to making sure the task is completed by the due date. Each week, your summary should be around 300 words long. Please take your obligations to act professionally seriously. When you are admitted as a lawyer, you undertake to act as an officer of the court. This responsibility is taken seriously by the Legal Practitioners Admissions Board. Any offence or academic misconduct you commit can compromise your capacity to be admitted, or stay admitted as a legal practitioner. Professional honesty and integrity are fundamental professional values which must be respected now, and for the rest of your legal career. I am relying on you, and your partner, to be honest with me. Don’t agree to lie for anyone – it is not a good start to your career. Students will receive a grade of: 0, 5 or 10. To receive a 10, students must: • genuinely reflect on the readings with your friend and write detailed noted about what you discussed and the conclusions you came to; • write around 300-400 words for each conversation; • refer to the readings, however no formal referencing is required. All four template forms must be submitted via the Blackboard site by Friday 30 October at 2pm. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.due_date: 11/09/2026 - 14/09/2026 Students will book a time for their oral presentation on Friday 11 Sept, Sunday 13 Sept or Monday 14 Sept.
assessment_details.task_description: Students will deliver an oral presentation in a private meeting with Prof Walsh. The presentation will be recorded. Students will present an opening address for a client. Facts will be provided well in advance. The opening address will be no more than 5 minutes’ duration. Students will then be asked one or two questions to demonstrate their understanding of the case. Students must submit a script – a written version of their opening address – at the meeting. This does not have to be a word-for-word version of the presentation. It can be a series of dot points, for example. The script should not be longer than 750 words, and should not exceed two pages. Students will be invited to book a timeslot with Prof Walsh on: Friday 11 September, Sunday 13 September of Monday 14 September. Students can receive a maximum mark of 30. The oral presentation is worth 30% of students’ final grade. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 2 To Week 13 (03 Aug - 01 Nov)
learning_activities.topic: Seminars The seminar topics are: Week 1 - Overview of the course | Video only (no classes) Week 2 - Human rights law: Who needs it? Week 3 - International human rights law: Historic human rights instruments and taking a rights-based approach Week 4 - Rights in Australian law (Commonwealth) Week 5 - Human Rights Acts in Australia Week 6 - Human Rights in Queensland: Rights in Australian law Week 7 - Human rights dispute resolution Week 8 - Oral presentations (no classes) Week 9 - Introduction to Anti-Discrimination Law | Video only (no classes): International approaches to human rights law Week 10 - Race discrimination and human rights of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples Week 11 - Sex discrimination and sexual harassment Week 12 - Disability discrimination: The Victorian Charter Week 13 - Other grounds of discrimination Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
